quote:

From him [came] a famous son, endowed with all virtues — a god-devotee named Gandal (Gondal), a giver (*dana*), an enjoyer (*bhokta*), discerning, and conqueror of all enemies, who became renowned by his fame."
In the third shloka is — "His son Pata (Jnata), by churning the enemy armies (*arivala-mathan*), obtained the kingdom, and won fame in keeping with the ancestors of the lineage. Upon the earthly sphere, going to Madhyadesh Malava, he attained renown; of a movement conforming to [his] branch, a god-worshipper, having performed religious austerity (*dharma-tapasya*), he built temples furnished with water-reservoirs."

book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
quote: But in the writings of Kakanadabot (Sanchi) and Udayagiri, respectively, Amrakardava *[the source reads "आत्रकादवर्द" — garbled]* and Virasena *["शाब" is unclear in source]* — who were the emperor's trusted commanders — were called the *tat-padanudhyata* of Chandragupta II Vikramaditya. From this it was concluded that the literal meaning, "meditating upon the feet," is more apt. This is a eulogy of praise, which has nothing to do with succession. book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
quote: Now the last knot that remains is this: if King Bhoj and King Udayadity were both "*sahodar*" (uterine brothers, born of the same mother), then Udayadity's birth must have occurred before the death of their father King Sindhuraj, or within just a few months of that death. The exact date of King Sindhuraj's death is not known, but his son King Bhojdev appears as a king in Dhar in 1011 CE. If they were uterine brothers, then Udayadity ought, in the ordinary course, to have become king after King Bhojdev's death in 1055 CE. Why did he have to wait until 1070 CE?

quote: It was a small place situated five hundred kilometres from Dhar, the capital of the Paramaras, on their border — which certainly had strategic importance in the sense that it touched the territory of the Kalachuri dynasty. Udaipur became an important centre situated on the frontier of the two dynasties because there were sandstone quarries here. Being under the Paramaras, Udaipur had seen itself developing like some mini-capital. Its importance lay in this — that a future emperor of the Paramara dynasty had, in his youth, lived in Udaipur. That crown-prince was Udayaditya, whose coronation the city of Dhara once witnessed — that same city of Dhara which was King Bhoj's beloved city; today's Dhar, the magnificent capital of the Paramaras.

book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
quote: It is very possible that Crown-Prince Udayaditya was sent, in his father's time, to Udaipur situated on the border of the Paramaras' kingdom. It may be that Udayaditya himself made the first major plan for the development of this frontier town and, according to the tradition of his lineage, began the finest constructions, which must have continued even after he became king. Otherwise, such temples are there village by village, but the layout of a palace encircled by a vast boundary wall and bastions, within a town protected by a square fort, is only there in this region. It must certainly have been a settlement inhabited before Udayaditya, where the Paramaras' military detachment must have been posted for the protection of the borders. Udayaditya's appointment had awakened the fortune of this settlement, where now something was going to happen that would remain alive in memory even after centuries.

book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
quote: In the old settlement of today's Vidisha, the most special of all is that very Vijay Mandir, which was built by the Paramara king Narvarman. In the genealogy of the Paramaras, king Narvarman's order comes after king Udayaditya; he was his successor. It is possible that at the time of the construction of Udaipur's Neelkantheshwar Mahadev temple, the young Narvarman lived in Udaipur itself, and that, after taking up the affairs of state in the capital Dhar, his inclination remained toward this region.
tier_note: T8 tradition / testimony: testimony and local tradition (Tiwari); memory, not the event; pages approximate

book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
quote:
Whichever king may have had it started, I feel he wanted to leave behind his predecessor king Udayaditya — exactly like king Narvarman, who, by building the Vijay Mandir in Vidisha, tried to go several steps ahead of his father's great construction work in Udaipur.
It is possible that he was going to create something four steps ahead of even Narvarman's Vijay Mandir.

book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
quote: It is very possible that this is an episode of the later period of the Paramaras. Whatever emerged, emerged as much as it could and stopped right there. In Udaipur's fate, only this much of what the Paramaras did was written.

book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
quote: In the form of the Vijay Mandir, Maharaj Udayaditya's son, and the 13th Maharaj of the Paramara dynasty, Narvarman, made in Vidisha a construction vaster and grander than his father's. But it could last only a hundred years. The great father's creation stands proudly even after a thousand years.

book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
quote: Worthy of note, too, is that long before the date of the inscription, Devpaldev had already begun sitting upon the royal throne in the capital Dhar and using the full royal titles. Before becoming king, he must have held some military or administrative responsibility in Udaipur itself — and that is why, in this inscription, he is addressed only with the title of *Mahakumar*. If he was in Udaipur before becoming king, then this fact enhances the importance of Udaipur; for, about a hundred and fifty years before him, Udayadity too must have been in some such role. Now this also becomes clear — that Udaipur was such a centre from which at least two crown-princes came forth to become kings in the Paramara dynasty.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
अपने पाँच शताब्दियों के लम्बे काल में महात्वाकांक्षी परमार राजाओं ने एक बड़े भूभाग पर अपनी सीमाओं का विस्तार किया। उनका राज्य मालवा के साथ भोपाल के आगे विदिशा और उदयपुर तक, पश्चिम में हंसोल, मोढासा, महुडी जैसे इलाकों तक फैला हुआ था। दक्षिण में नर्मदा के तटीय क्षेत्रों जैसे होशंगाबाद से लेकर उत्तर में कोटा तक के इलाकों पर परमार राज कर रहे थे।
*Gloss [my translation]:* In their long period of five centuries ambitious Paramara kings expanded their borders over a large area. Their kingdom spread with Malwa beyond Bhopal to Vidisha and Udaypur, in the west to areas like Hansol, Modasa and Mahudi. Paramaras ruled areas from Hoshangabad on the Narmada coast in the south to Kota in the north.

quote:
की गाय का बलात् हरण किया, तब उन (वसिष्ठ) के प्रभाव से अग्निकुण्ड में से एक
वीर उत्पन्न हुआ जिसने अकेले ही शत्रु सैन्य का नाश किया ॥५॥
मारयित्वा परान्धेनुमानिन्ये स ततो मुनिः।
उवाच परमारा [ख्यः पा]थिवेंद्रो भविष्यसि ॥६॥
शत्रुओं को मार कर वह गाय को वापस ले आया, तब मुनि ने कहा--"तुम परमार
नाम से राजा होगे ॥६॥
*Gloss [my translation]:* ... when (he) forcibly took away the cow, then through the influence of (Vasishtha) a hero arose from the fire-pit who alone destroyed the enemy army. Having killed the enemies he brought back the cow; then the sage said: 'You will be a king by the name Paramara.'

quote:
उस वंश में अखिल यज्ञ समूह से तूभ देवताओं के द्वारा जिसकी कीर्ति गाई जा रही
है व जो द्विज समूह में रत्न के समान हैं और जिसने अपने पराक्रम से उच्च राजत्व का
मान प्राप्त कर लिया है ऐसा उपेन्द्रराज (नरेश) हुआ ॥७॥
*Gloss [my translation]:* In that lineage was born Upendraraja, whose fame is sung by the gods and who is like a jewel among the twice-born, and who by his valour has attained the dignity of high kingship.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
उसका पुत्र बैरिसिंह था जो राजारूपी हाथियों के लिये सिंह के समान था, जो
पराक्रमियों में सबसे बलवान था और जिसने चारों समुद्रों से युक्त पृथ्वी पर प्रशस्तियुक्त
जयस्तम्भ स्थापित किये !!८॥
*Gloss [my translation]:* His son was Vairisimha, who was like a lion to elephant-like kings, strongest among the valiant, and who set up victory pillars with prashastis on the earth bounded by the four seas.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
उसके श्री सीयक (उत्पन्न) हुआ जिसका पादपीठ पृथ्वी के नरेशों के मुकुटों के
रत्नप्रभा से रंजित होता था तथा जिसकी तलवार की जल लहरियों में शत्रुसमूह डूब
जाते थे, जो विजयी राजाओं में सर्वश्रेष्ठ था ॥९॥
तस्माद्वन्ति तरूणीय नारविन्दभारवान्भूत्करकृपाणगरीचिदीपः।
श्रीवाक्यपतिः स (श) तमरवान्कृतितुरंगा गंगासमुद्र सलिलानि पि वन्ति यस्मै ॥१०॥
उससे श्री वाक्यपति हुआ जो अवन्ति की युवतियों के नयन कमलों के लिये सूर्य के समान था, अपने हाथ की तलवार की चमक से जो स्वयं प्रकाशमान था, जो इन्द्र के समान था तथा जिसके अक्ष गंगा व समुद्र के जलों का पान करते थे ॥१०॥
*Gloss [my translation]:* From him was born Shri Siyaka, whose footstool was coloured by the jewel-radiance of the crowns of the kings of the earth and in whose sword's water-waves enemy hosts drowned, the foremost of victorious kings. From him came Shri Vakpati, who was like the sun to the lotus-eyes of the young women of Avanti, self-radiant with the gleam of the sword in his hand, like Indra, and whose horses drank the waters of the Ganga and the sea.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
उसका पुत्र जो संपूर्ण पृथ्वी के लिये आभूषण रूप था, जो गुणों का एकमात्र आश्रय था, शौर्य से जीते समस्त शत्रुओं से धन प्राप्ति के द्वारा जिसके कोप में वृद्धि होती थी, जो वकृत्य, उच्च कवित्व, तर्क प्रवीणता तथा शास्त्र आगम में निष्णात था तथा सज्जनों के द्वारा श्रीमत् वाक्यपतिराजदेव के नाम से जिसकी कीर्ति गाई जाती है ॥१३॥
कर्णाटलाटकैरल चोलशिरोरन्तरागिपदकमलः।
यशः प्रणीयगणार्थितदाता कल्पवृक्षप्रख्यः ॥१४॥
जिसके पदकमल कर्णाट लाट केरल चोल (नरेशों) के मुकुट रत्नों से रंजित होते थे और जो प्रार्थना करने वाले याचकों की इच्छा पूर्ति के लिये कल्पवृक्ष के समान विख्यात था ॥१४॥
*Gloss [my translation]:* His son, an ornament for the whole earth, sole refuge of virtues, whose wrath grew by wealth taken from enemies conquered in valour, skilled in oratory, high poetry, logic and the scriptures, whose fame is sung by good men by the name of Shrimat Vakpatirajadeva. Whose lotus feet were coloured by the crown jewels of Karnata, Lata, Kerala and Chola kings, and who was known as a wish-fulfilling tree for petitioners.

quote:
त्रिपुरी नगरी में विजय की इच्छा करने वाले उसने युद्ध में युवराज को जीतकर तथा उसके सेनापतियों को मार कर अपनी खड्ग को ऊंचा किया ॥१५॥

quote:
उसके छोटे भाई श्री सिंधुराज ने हूणराज को जीत कर विजयश्री प्राप्त की, जिससे भोजराज उत्पन्न हुआ, जिसने उत्तम व्यक्तियों को भी कंपा दिया व जो अद्वितीय रत्न था ॥१६॥
*Gloss [my translation]:* His younger brother Shri Sindhuraja won victory by conquering the Huna king, from whom was born Bhojaraja, who made even excellent men tremble and who was a unique jewel.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
जिसने कैलाश से मलय तक तथा उदयाचल से अस्ताचल तक संपूर्ण पृथ्वी का पृथुराज के समान उपभोग किया, जिसने अपने धनुष की डोरी से सहज ही में दिक्पालों को उखाड़ कर दिशाओं में फेंक दिया तथा जिसने पृथ्वी को परमप्रीति से प्रसन्न किया ॥१७॥
साधितं विहितं दत्तं ज्ञातं तथान्य केनचित्।
किमन्यत्कविराजस्य श्रीभोजस्य प्रशस्यते ॥१८॥
जो उसने साधित किया (प्राप्त किया), जो आदेश किया, जो दिया, जो ज्ञात किया वह कोई न कर सका। कविराज श्री भोज की इससे अधिक प्रशंसा क्या हो सकती है ॥१८॥
*Gloss [my translation]:* He who enjoyed the entire earth from Kailasa to Malaya and from the rising mountain to the setting mountain like Prithu, who easily uprooted the guardians of the directions with his bowstring and threw them in the directions, and who gladdened the earth with supreme love. What he achieved, ordained, gave and knew, none else could do. What more praise can there be of Kaviraja Shri Bhoja.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
कर्णाट, लाटपति, गुर्जर नरेश व तुर्कों, जिनमें मुख्य चेदि नरेश इन्द्रथ, तोगल तथा भीम थे, की सेनाओं को जिसके भृत्यमात्रों ने ही विजित कर लिया व इस कारण जिसके पारंपरिक सेनाओं के बाहुबल की उन्नता की गणना की जाती है, उसके योद्धाओं की नहीं की जाती (क्योंकि योद्धाओं की तो अभी बारी भी नहीं आ पाई थी) ॥१९॥
*Gloss [my translation]:* The armies of the Karnata, the lord of Lata, the Gurjara king and the Turks, chiefly the Chedi king Indratha, Togala and Bhima, were conquered by his mere servants, and so the strength of his traditional armies is counted, not that of his warriors (since the warriors had not yet had their turn).

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
यह परमार राजाओं के महान कृतित्व की कहानी है, जिसकी शान में उदयादित्य नाम के राजा भोज के उत्तराधिकारी ने चार चांद लगा दिए थे।
*Gloss [my translation]:* This is the story of the great works of the Paramara kings, to whose glory Udayaditya, a successor of King Bhoja, added lustre.

quote:
आखिर उदयपुर का भी तो राजा भोज से गहरा रिश्ता है। उदयादित्य उनके ही बाद में तो महाराजा हुए थे। उदयपुर के विकास की हर रूपरेखा से भोज भलीभांति अवगत रहे होंगे। उदयादित्य ने उनके ही संरक्षण में खुद को अपनी समृद्ध अभिरुचियों के साथ कुशल राजकाज के लिए तैयार किया होगा।
*Gloss [my translation]:* After all, Udaipur too has a deep relationship with Raja Bhoj. Udayaditya became maharaja after him. Bhoj must have been well aware of every outline of Udaipur's development. Udayaditya must have prepared himself for skilled governance with his rich interests under Bhoj's patronage.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
जिन राजा उदयदित्य के नाम पर इस नगर का नामकरण हुआ, वे परमार राजवंश के 12 वें राजा हैं। राजा भोज के बंधु हैं। यानी राजकाज के तौर-तरीके उन्होंने राजा भोज के साथ ही सीखे-समझे होंगे और जब राजा भोज राजधानी धार से अपना साम्राज्य देखते होंगे तब उदयदित्य को यहां का सामंत बनाकर भेजा गया होगा।
*Gloss [my translation]:* King Udayaditya, after whom this town is named, is the 12th king of the Paramara dynasty. He is King Bhoja's brother. That is, he must have learned and understood the ways of governance along with King Bhoja, and when King Bhoja was overseeing his empire from the capital Dhar, Udayaditya must have been sent here as feudatory.

quote:
यह भी परमारों के दूसरे शिलालेखों की तरह शिव की आराधना से शुरू है और आगे उदयাদित्य के बारे में बताना शुरू कर देता है। हर शिलालेख कुछ नई जानकारी देता है। कुछ अलग इशारे करता है। यह भोज और उदयাদित्य के बीच के समय की धुंध में अस्पष्ट से दिखाई देने वाले संबंधों पर नई रोशनी डालता है।
इसके दूसरे श्लोक में है-"श्रीमान पावर (परमार) वंश नरेश सूरवीर मालव राज्य स्थापित करने वाला विद्वान नरेश हुआ जो पापियों को दण्डित करता था। उससे प्रसिद्ध पुत्र सकल गुणों से युक्त गांडल (गोंडल) नामक देवभक्त, दाना, भोक्ता, विवेकी और समस्त शत्रुओं को जीत वाला, अपनी कीर्ति से विख्यात हुआ।"
*Gloss [my translation]:* Like other Paramara inscriptions it begins with worship of Shiva and goes on to tell about Udayaditya. Each inscription gives some new information. It throws new light on the relation between Bhoja and Udayaditya, seen faintly in the haze of time. Its second verse says a heroic, learned Paramara king established the Malwa kingdom and punished sinners. From him a renowned son named Gandal (Gondal), devout, generous, discerning, who conquered all enemies, became famous for his glory.

quote:
यह भी हो सकता है कि जब कल्याणी के चालुक्यों और कर्णटों की संयुक्त सेनाओं ने राजधानी धारा पर हमलाकर भोजदेव के पुत्र और उत्तराधिकारी जयसिंह प्रथम को 1070 ई. के आसपास युद्ध में मार दिया हो तो ऐसी स्थिति में अचानक पैदा हुए राजनीतिक खालीपन में उदयাদित्य सिंहासन पर आए हों। यह सवाल और अहम है कि उदयাদित्य का राजा भोज से रिश्ता क्या था?
*Gloss [my translation]:* It may also be that when the combined armies of the Chalukyas of Kalyani and the Karnatas attacked the capital Dhara and killed Bhoja's son and successor Jayasimha I around 1070 CE, Udayaditya came to the throne in the sudden political vacuum. The question of Udayaditya's relation to Raja Bhoja is more important.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
वे कहते हैं कि उदयাদित्य के पिता के रूप में इन 'पाता' अथवा 'ज्ञाता' का जिक्र नए इशारे करने वाला बिंदु है। इसका एक मतलब यह है कि उदयাদित्य सिंधुराज की वंशपरम्परा से नहीं आ रहे थे बल्कि परमार राजवंश की एक अवर-शाखा से संबंधित थे। इसके आधार पर ऐसा माना जा सकता है कि उदयাদित्य संभवतः महाराजा भोज के अधीन एक सामंतान्धिपति के रूप में मालवा के पूर्वी भाग में राज करते थे। इस इलाके में विदिशा भी था। तब उदयपुर इसके अंतर्गत एक महत्वपूर्ण केंद्र के रूप में विकसित होने लगा होगा।
*Gloss [my translation]:* Verma stops here to analyse. He says that the mention of 'Pata' or 'Jnata' as Udayaditya's father is a point suggesting new indications. One meaning is that Udayaditya did not descend from Sindhuraja's line but belonged to a junior branch of the Paramara dynasty. On this basis it can be assumed that Udayaditya probably ruled in the eastern part of Malwa as a chief feudatory under Maharaja Bhoja. Vidisha was also in this region. Then Udaypur must have begun to develop under it as an important centre.

quote:
अर्थात् "शिवभक्त (भोजदेव), जिसका प्रताप सूर्य के समान था, के स्वर्ग चले जाने पर, धारा नगरी के समान जब सारी पृथ्वी शत्रुरूपी अंधकार से व्याप्त हो गई तथा उसके पारंपरिक योद्धाजन दुर्बल हो गये, तब सूर्य के समान उदयादित्यदेव,
उन्नत शत्रूपी अंधकार को खड्गदण्ड की किरणों से नष्ट कर समस्तजनों के मनो को आनन्दित करता हुआ, उदित हुआ।
*Gloss [my translation]:* After the Shiva-devotee (Bhojadeva), whose glory was like the sun, went to heaven, when the whole earth like the city of Dhara was covered by the darkness of enemies and his traditional warriors had grown weak, then Udayadityadeva, like the sun, rose, destroying the towering darkness of enemies with the rays of his sword and gladdening all people.

यस्योदयादित्य नृपः पितासी, देवः पितृव्यः स च भोजराजः ।

quote:
नागपुर अभिलेख राजा उदयादित्य के पुत्र राजा नरवर्मन का है जो उदयादित्य के बाद 1094 में परमार वंश के अगले राजा हुए और 1133 ई० तक शासन किया। इसमें परमार राजवंश की नरवर्मन तक की पूरी जानकारी है कि कौन किसके बाद सिंहासन पर आया। 56 वें श्लोक में साफ है कि यह प्रशस्ति स्वयं राजा नरवर्मन के द्वारा रची गई थी।
*Gloss [my translation]:* The Nagpur inscription is of King Naravarman, son of King Udayaditya, who became the next king of the Paramara dynasty in 1094 after Udayaditya and ruled until 1133 CE. It has full information on the Paramara dynasty up to Naravarman, who succeeded whom. Verse 56 makes clear that this prashasti was composed by King Naravarman himself.

अर्थात् "उस (भोजदेव) के इन्द्र की बंधुता को प्राप्त (दिवंगत) होने पर और राज्यस्वामी के कौटुम्बिकों के संघर्षरूपी जल में मग्न होने पर, उसका बंधु उदयादित्य नरेश हुआ, जिसने महासागर के समान संयुक्त रूप से कर्णाट कर्ण आदि नृपतियों के द्वारा पीड़ित इस पृथ्वी का उद्धार कर के वराह अवतार का अनुकरण किया। इसमें उदयादित्य को भोजदेव का "बंधु" बताया गया है। यह ध्यान देने योग्य शब्द है। धर्मशास्त्र में तीन प्रकार के बंधु हैं-आत्मबन्धु, पितृबन्धु और मातृबन्धु। इसके अलावा नातेदार, भाई-बिरादरी, सम्बन्धी, पारिवारिक नातेदार भी बंधु कहलाते हैं।
*Gloss [my translation]:* After he (Bhojadeva) attained the kinship of Indra and the lord of the kingdom's kinsmen were sunk in the water of conflict, his bandhu Udayaditya became king, who, like the Varaha incarnation, rescued the earth troubled by the Karnata Karna and others joined like an ocean. Here Udayaditya is called Bhojadeva's 'bandhu'. This is a noteworthy word. In dharmashastra there are three kinds of bandhu: atmabandhu, pitribandhu and matribandhu. Besides, relatives, brotherhood and family kin are also called bandhu.

तारीख ज्ञात नहीं है परन्तु उनके पुत्र राजा भोजदेव 1011 ईस्वी में धार में एक राजा के

quote:
शिव भक्त (राजा भोज), जिसका प्रताप सूर्य के समान था, के स्वर्ग चले जाने पर धारा नगरी के समान सारी पृथ्वी शत्रु रूपी अंधकार से व्याप्त हो गई तथा उसके पारंपरिक योद्धाजन दुर्बल हो गये, तब सूर्य के समान उदयादित्यदेव उन्नत शत्रुरूप अंधकार को खड्गदण्ड की किरणों से नष्ट करके समस्त जनो के मनो को आनन्दित करता हुआ उदित हुआ।॥२१॥
येन धरणीवराहः परमारेशो[दृधुतो] निरायासा (तु) ।
तस्यतस्य भूमेरुद्दरो वत कियन्मात्रः ॥२२॥
जो (पृथ्वी उद्धार का) कार्य वराह अवतार ने किया, वह भूमि उद्धार का कार्य इस परमार ने कितनी सुगमता से किया, यह कितना आश्चर्य है ॥२२॥
*Gloss [my translation]:* After the Shiva-devotee (King Bhoja), whose glory was like the sun, went to heaven, the whole earth, like the city of Dhara, was covered with the darkness of enemies and his traditional warriors grew weak; then Udayadityadeva rose like the sun, destroying the towering darkness of enemies with the rays of his sword and delighting all people. The work of rescuing the earth that the Varaha avatar did, how easily this Paramara did it, how wonderful.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
चलते-चलते विदिशा के पास प्रसिद्ध उदयगिरि गुफाएँ, विदिशा से सतर किमी दूर उदयपुर और इसी नगर में उदयेश्वर महादेव देवालय के सामने करीब पाँच सौ मीटर दूर स्थित उदयसमुद्र आदि संज्ञाएँ परमारकालीन इतिहास में भोज के पौत्र के तौर पर
उल्लेखित उद्यादित्य के नाम पर ही हैं। कहीं कहीं उसका उल्लेख भोजबन्धु के रूप में भी है। हालाँकि सांची के समीप पाँचवीं सदी ईस्वी की गुफाओं का निर्माण उद्यादित्य ने नहीं कराया था। पहाड़ी को उसने अपना नाम दिया था।
*Gloss [my translation]:* Names such as the famous Udayagiri caves near Vidisha, Udaypur seventy km from Vidisha, and in this same town the Udayasamudra located about five hundred metres in front of the Udayeshvara Mahadeva temple are all after Udayaditya, who is mentioned in Paramara history as Bhoja's grandson. In some places he is also mentioned as Bhojabandhu. However, the fifth-century caves near Sanchi were not built by Udayaditya. He gave the hill his name.

In some places he is also mentioned as Bhojabandhu. However, the fifth-century caves near Sanchi were not built by Udayaditya. He gave the hill his name.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
महाराष्ट्र, गुजरात और राजस्थान के भीतर से लेकर परमारों के राज्य की उत्तर दिशा में सीमा यहां उदयपुर तक विस्तृत थी। यहां से कलचुरियों का इलाका शुरू होता था। उदयपुर सीमा पर होने की वजह से परमारों के लिए सामरिक दृष्टि से बहुत अहम रहा होगा, जो कि इसके एक हज़ार साल पुराने विकास और विस्तार से जाहिर भी है।
*Gloss [my translation]:* From within Maharashtra, Gujarat and Rajasthan, the northern limit of the Paramara kingdom extended up to Udaipur here. From here the Kalachuri territory began. Being on the border, Udaipur must have been strategically very important for the Paramaras, as its thousand-year-old development and expansion also show.
tier_note: T8 tradition / testimony: testimony and local tradition (Tiwari); memory, not the event
gloss: From within Maharashtra, Gujarat and Rajasthan, the northern limit of the Paramara kingdom extended up to Udaipur here. From here the Kalachuri territory began. Being on the border, Udaipur must have been strategically very important for the Paramaras, as its thousand-year-old development and expansion also show.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
यह तो किसी राज्य की राजधानी भी नहीं था। वह परमारों की राजधानी धार से पांच सौ किलोमीटर दूर उनकी सीमा पर स्थित एक छोटा सा स्थान था, जिसका सामरिक महत्व इस नाते जरूर था कि वह कलचुरि राजवंश के क्षेत्र को छूता था। उदयपुर दोनों राजवंशों की सरहद पर स्थित एक महत्वपूर्ण केंद्र इसलिए बन गया कि यहां बलुआ पत्थर की खदानें थीं। परमारों के मातहत होने से उदयपुर ने किसी मिनी केपिटल की तरह खुद को विकसित होते हुए देखा था।
*Gloss [my translation]:* This was not even the capital of any state. It was a small place on the Paramāra border, five hundred kilometres from their capital Dhar, whose strategic importance was that it touched the Kalachuri dynasty's territory. Udaypur became an important centre on the border of both dynasties because there were sandstone quarries here.
tier_note: T8 tradition / testimony: testimony and local tradition (Tiwari); memory, not the event

claim.value: on the Paramāra frontier, 500 km from Dhar (as stated)

gloss: This was not even the capital of any state. It was a small place on the Paramāra border, five hundred kilometres from their capital Dhar, whose strategic importance was that it touched the Kalachuri dynasty's territory. book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
परमारों के मातहत होने से उदयपुर ने किसी मिनी केपिटल की तरह खुद को विकसित होते हुए देखा था। इसका महत्व इसी में था कि परमार राजवंश का एक भविष्य सम्राट अपनी युवावस्था में उदयपुर में रहा था। वह युवराज उदयादित्य थे, जिनका राज्याभिषेक कभी धारा नगरी ने देखा। वही धारा नगरी जो राजा भोज की प्रिय नगरी थी।
*Gloss [my translation]:* Under the Paramāras, Udaypur saw itself developing like a mini capital. Its importance lay in this: a future emperor of the Paramāra dynasty lived in Udaypur in his youth. That prince was Udayāditya, whose coronation Dhara city once witnessed. The same Dhara city that was King Bhoja's favourite city.
tier_note: T8 tradition / testimony: testimony and local tradition (Tiwari); memory, not the event
gloss: Under the Paramāras, Udaypur saw itself developing like a mini capital. Its importance lay in this: a future emperor of the Paramāra dynasty lived in Udaypur in his youth. book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
बहुत संभव है युवराज उदयादित्य अपने पिता के समय परमारों के राज्य की सीमा पर स्थित उदयपुर भेजे गए हों। हो सकता है कि उदयादित्य ने ही इस सीमावर्ती नगर के विकास की पहली बड़ी योजना बनाई हो और अपनी वंश परंपरा के अनुसार बेहतरीन निर्माण शुरू किए हों, जो उनके राजा बनने के बाद भी जारी रहे होंगे।
*Gloss [my translation]:* It is quite possible that prince Udayāditya was sent to Udaypur, on the border of the Paramāra kingdom, in his father's time. It may be that Udayāditya himself made the first major plan for developing this border town and began excellent constructions as per his dynastic tradition, which continued after he became king.

quote:
इस जगह की प्रसिद्धि नीलकंठेश्वर मंदिर से है, जो राजा भोज के बाद की पीढ़ी में हुए महाराज उदयादित्य ने बनवाया था। इस नगर का नाम उदयपुर भी उनसे ही जुड़ा है।
*Gloss [my translation]:* This place is famous for the Nilakantheshwar temple, which Maharaja Udayaditya, of the generation after King Bhoja, had built. The name of this town, Udaypur, is also connected with him.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
उदयपुर एक गहरी शोध परियोजना का हिस्सा हो सकता है, जिसमें राजा भोज की नगर रचना एक महत्वपूर्ण विषय है। यह चौकोर आकार में चारों तरफ से बराबर लंबी दीवारों से घिरा एक शानदार नगर रहा है, जिसके भीतर राजा के महल का होना बताता है कि यहां भोज के वारिस रहे ही होंगे और वो उद्यादित्य ही हैं, जिनके नाम से यह नगर है।
*Gloss [my translation]:* Udaypur could be part of a deep research project in which King Bhoja's town planning is an important subject. It has been a splendid town in a square shape enclosed by walls of equal length on all sides, the presence of a king's palace inside which shows that Bhoja's heirs must have been here, and that is Udayaditya, after whom the town is named.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
उदयदित्य ने उदयपुर में रहते हुए अपनी गौरवशाली राज परंपरा को ही बढ़ाया था। यही वजह है कि सदियां बीतने के बावजूद वे अब तक इस पूरे क्षेत्र की स्मृतियों मैं जगमगा रहे हैं...
*Gloss [my translation]:* Udayaditya, while living in Udaypur, carried forward his glorious royal tradition. That is why, even after centuries, he still glows in the memories of this entire region.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
उदयपुर परमार राजवंश की भौगोलिक सीमा पर था, जो सामरिक दृष्टि से महत्वपूर्ण था। चारों तरफ दुर्ग से घिरे उदयपुर से सटे पहाड़ पर भी एक किलेबंदी के अवशेष गूगल मैप से भी दिखाई देते हैं। मुख्य मंदिर के अलावा राजमहल के विशाल परिसर की मौजूदगी बताती है कि परमार राजाओं के परिजन अपनी इस सीमा की सुरक्षा के लिए स्वयं रहे होंगे।
*Gloss [my translation]:* Udaypur was on the geographic border of the Paramara dynasty, which was strategically important. Remains of a fortification on the hill adjoining Udaypur, surrounded on all sides by a fort, are visible even on Google Map. Besides the main temple, the presence of the large palace complex shows that family members of the Paramara kings themselves must have been here for the security of this border.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
वर्मा अगला सवाल लेकर आते हैं कि उदयपुर का निर्माण वास्तव में किसने किया? उदयदित्य के समय का एक शिलालेख (उदयपुर प्रशस्ति का परवर्ती परंतु तिथि रहित) इस बारे में कुछ कीमती सुराग देता है। लेकिन इसका आधे से ज्यादा हिस्सा अत्यधिक क्षतिग्रस्त हो जाने के कारण पढ़ने लायक नहीं बचा। इस पर कोई तिथि भी नहीं है। हो सकता है वह उस हिस्से में रही हो जो बरबाद हो गया। इसकी अहमियत यही है कि यह उदयपुर नगर और मंदिर के बारे में हमें रोककर कुछ सुराग देता है।
*Gloss [my translation]:* Verma brings the next question: who actually built Udaypur? An inscription of Udayaditya's time (later than the Udaypur prashasti but undated) gives some valuable clues about this. But more than half of it has become unreadable because of heavy damage. It has no date either. Perhaps it was in the part that was destroyed. Its importance is that it gives clues about the town of Udaypur and the temple.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
जहां तक उदयपुर की बात है तो इसके नाम से ही जाहिर है कि यह राजा उदयादित्य से संबंधित है। पूर्ववर्ती परमार राजाओं के किसी भी अभिलेख का यहां न मिलना यह बताता है कि यह नगर उदयादित्य के समय में ही अस्तित्व में आया।
*Gloss [my translation]:* As far as Udaypur is concerned, its very name shows it is related to King Udayaditya. That no inscription of earlier Paramara kings is found here shows that this town came into existence in Udayaditya's time.
tier_note: T8 tradition / testimony: testimony and local tradition (Tiwari); memory, not the event

claim.value: founded in Udayaditya's time; named after him; no earlier Paramara records here

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
पहली से छठवी पंक्ति में उदयादित्य की कुछ महत्वपूर्ण सैन्य विजयों का वर्णन है। इन विजितों में नाम केवल ढाहलमण्डल के चेदि शासक "ढाहलाधीश" का ही है। शिलालेख में दर्ज है कि ढहलाधीश को हराकर मार डाला गया। ढाहल मूलतः जबलपुर के आसपास का इलाका था जो कलचुरियों का मूलस्थान माना जाता है।
*Gloss [my translation]:* Lines one to six describe some important military victories of Udayaditya. Among these conquered the name only of the Chedi ruler of Dhahala-mandala, the 'Dhahaladhisha', is given. It is recorded in the inscription that the Dhahaladhisha was defeated and killed. Dhahala was originally the area around Jabalpur, which is considered the original home of the Kalachuris.

quote:
इस पर कोई तिथि अंकित नहीं है परन्तु इस अभिलेख से प्राप्त जानकारी के अनुसार यह राजा भोज के उत्तराधिकारी राजा उद्यादित्य के काल का प्रतीत होता है। राजा उद्यादित्य का शासनकाल 1070 से 1093 के बीच रहा।
*Gloss [my translation]:* No date is marked on it but according to information from this inscription it appears to be of the time of King Udayaditya, successor of King Bhoja. King Udayaditya's reign was between 1070 and 1093.

quote:
उदयपुर को उदयदित्य ने अपने पूरे मनोयोग से रचा था। राजा भोज के ये वंशज राज्य के इस आखिरी छोर का राज्यपाल थे। उसने उदयसागर बनवाया। नीलकंठेश्वर मंदिर खड़ा किया। देश के सुंदरतम देवालयों में से एक। स्थापत्य का बेजोड़ नमूना।
*Gloss [my translation]:* Udayaditya had created Udaypur with his full heart. This descendant of Raja Bhoja was the governor at this last edge of the state. He had Udayasagar built. He raised the Nilakantheshwar temple. One of the most beautiful temples of the country. A matchless specimen of architecture.

quote:
भूमिपूजन, शिलान्यास और गर्भगृह में अभिषेक का वह उत्सव, जब महाराज उदयादित्य स्वयं अपने मंत्रियों सहित सपरिवार यहां उपस्थित थे। धारा नगरी, उज्जयिनी, मंडपदुर्ग और भोपाल से भी अनेक प्रमुख सामंत और शिल्पी अपने शिष्यों के साथ यहां आए थे।
*Gloss [my translation]:* The festival of bhumipujan, foundation-laying and abhisheka in the sanctum, when Maharaj Udayaditya himself was present with ministers and family. Many chief feudatories and craftsmen with their pupils came from Dhara city, Ujjayini, Mandapadurga and Bhopal.

quote:
यहीं रहकर अपने राजा के लिए सदैव शुभकामनाएं व्यक्त की हों और जब मंदिर का निर्माण पूर्ण हुआ होगा तब उसने 30 मार्च 1080 के ध्वजारोहण समारोह के समय राजा के रथों का इंतजार किया हो। उदयपुर के राजमहलों की वह रौनक भी आखिरी नहीं थी। ढाई सौ साल बाद तक उदयपुर ऐसा ही चमकता रहा था।
*Gloss [my translation]:* When the temple's construction was complete she may have waited for the king's chariots at the flag-hoisting ceremony of 30 March 1080. That splendour of Udaipur's palaces was not the last. Udaipur kept shining like this for another two and a half hundred years.

quote:
इस शिलालेख की बाद की पंक्तियों में परमारों के अधीन किन्हीं नेमक वंश के स्थानीय नरेशों का विवरण है। चूंकि उदयपुर सीधा परमार शासन के अंतर्गत था तो ऐसा कैसे मुमकिन है कि किसी और वंश का जिक्र आए। मुमकिन है कि राजा उदयादित्य ने अपने मातहत नेमक वंशीय किसी सामंत को यह इलाका सौंप रखा हो। इस अधूरे शिलालेख में हो सकता है कि नेमकों के बारे में और कुछ ब्यौरे भी रहे हों, लेकिन वे पढ़े जाने लायक नहीं बचे।
*Gloss [my translation]:* In the later lines of this inscription there is an account of local rulers of a Nemaka dynasty under the Paramaras. Since Udaypur was under direct Paramara rule, how could another dynasty be mentioned? It is possible that King Udayaditya had assigned this area to a feudatory of the Nemaka lineage. Perhaps this incomplete inscription had more details about the Nemakas, but they have not survived to be read.

quote:
यह अभिलेख बताता है कि नेमक वंशीय शासक शिव के उपासक थे। शूद्रक नामक एक अन्य सामंत हुआ, जिसने किसी गुर्जर नरेश पर विजय प्राप्त की थी। इस अभिलेख में वर्णन है कि इसी शूद्रक नामक सामंत के पुत्र जिसका नाम अस्पष्ट है, ने उदयपुर में मंदिर का निर्माण करवाया था। हम यह अंदाजा ही लगा सकते हैं कि जिस समय उदयपुर मंदिर का निर्माण शुरू हुआ होगा, नेमक वंश का यह सामन्तकुल यहां का स्थानीय प्रशासक रहा हो और उसी की देखरेख में इस मंदिर का निर्माण हुआ हो।
*Gloss [my translation]:* This inscription tells that the Nemaka-line rulers were worshippers of Shiva. Another feudatory named Shudraka defeated some Gurjara king. The inscription describes that the son of this Shudraka, whose name is unclear, had a temple built at Udaypur. We can only guess that when construction of the Udaypur temple began, this feudatory family of the Nemaka line may have been the local administrator here and the temple was built under its supervision.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
हम अच्छी तरह से जानते हैं कि महात्वाकांक्षी परमार राजाओं की प्रसिद्धि उनकी वीरता और युद्ध विजयों के कारण ही नहीं है। उनके समय ज्ञान की सभी विधाओं को आसरा मिला। स्थापत्य के बेजोड़ स्मारक सदियों तक बनते ही रहे। इन स्मारकों के आसपास उज्जैन, धारा, मांडू, भोजपाल, विदिशा और उदयपुर तक बड़े नॉलेज सेंटर बने, जिन्हें इन राजाओं ने ऊंचाइयों तक पहुंचाया।
*Gloss [my translation]:* We know well that the fame of ambitious Paramara kings is not only for valour and conquests. In their time all branches of knowledge found shelter. Unmatched monuments of architecture were built for centuries. Around these monuments big knowledge centres arose up to Ujjain, Dhara, Mandu, Bhojpal, Vidisha and Udaypur, which these kings raised to heights.

जिसने चारों ओर केदारेश्वर, रामेश्वर, सोमनाथ, सुंदीर, काल, अनल व रुद्र आदि मंदिरों का निर्माण कर पवित्र पृथ्वी को यथार्थ नाम वाली बनाया ॥२०॥

बहुत मुमकिन है कि यह परमारों के उत्तराध्य का प्रसंग हो। जो जितना उभर पाया था वह वहीं ठहर गया। उदयपुर के भाग्य में परमारों का किया हुआ इतना ही लिखा था।

quote:
विजय मंदिर के रूप में महाराज उदयदित्य के बेटे और परमार राजवंश के 13 वें महाराज नरवर्मन ने विदिशा में अपने पिता से विशाल और भव्य निर्माण किया था। मगर वह सिर्फ सौ साल ही रह पाया। महान पिता की रचना एक हज़ार साल बाद भी शान से खड़ी है।
*Gloss [my translation]:* As Vijay Mandir, Naravarman, son of Maharaj Udayaditya and the 13th king of the Paramara dynasty, made a bigger and grander construction than his father at Vidisha. But it survived only a hundred years. The great father's creation still stands proudly after a thousand years.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
ध्यान देने वाली यह भी है कि अभिलेख की तिथि से बहुत पहले देवपालदेव राजधानी धार में राजसिंहासन पर बैठकर पूर्ण राजकीय उपाधियों का उपयोग करने लगे थे। वे राजा बनने के पहले उदयपुर में ही किसी सैन्य या प्रशासनिक जिम्मेदारी में रहे होंगे और इसीलिए इस अभिलेख में उन्हें महाकुमार की उपाधि से ही संबोधित किया गया है। अगर वे राजा बनने के पहले उदयपुर में रहे हैं तो यह तथ्य उदयपुर की अहमियत को बढ़ाने वाला है क्योंकि उनसे करीब ढेढ़ सौ साल पहले उदयादित्य भी ऐसी किसी भूमिका में रहे होंगे। अब यह भी स्पष्ट हो जाता है कि उदयपुर एक ऐसा केंद्र था जहां से कम से कम दो युवराज तो परमार राजवंश में राजा बनकर निकले थे।
*Gloss [my translation]:* It is worth noting that long before the date of the inscription Devapaladeva had sat on the throne in the capital Dhar and begun using full royal titles. Before becoming king he must have held some military or administrative responsibility at Udaypur, and hence in this inscription he is addressed only by the title Mahakumara. If he lived at Udaypur before becoming king, this fact raises Udaypur's importance, because about a hundred and fifty years earlier Udayaditya too must have been in such a role. Now it also becomes clear that Udaypur was a centre from which at least two princes of the Paramara dynasty emerged as kings.

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: The inscription then proceeds to trace the genealogy of the Paramāra house of Mālwā. It tells us in vv. 5-6 that a hero who had sprung from the fire-altar of Vasishtha on the Mount Arbuda (Ābū) slew the enemies and brought back the cow of the sage which Viśvāmitra had taken away, and was, in reward of this deed, given the name of Paramāra (slayer of the foes) by Vasishtha who also blessed him with kingship. \( ^{2} \)  This account is purely legendary, a later creation, and can mean nothing more than to invent a high origin for the house, calling the Paramāras as belonging to agni-kula, exactly similar to that of the races born from the Sun and the moon. \( ^{3} \)  The present inscription, as we may note here, is the first to mention this legend, which is echoed in the later epigraphical records of the house, e.g., in the Nagpur Museum inscription and the Mändhātā copper-plate grant of Jayasimha II, as we shall see below.
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: Verses 8-11 mention the names of Vairisinha, Siyaka, Vākpati and another (a second) Vairisinha, each of whom was the son of his predecessor. The description here is purely conventional, except that we learn that the last of these rulers, viz., Vairisinha, was also known as Vajraṭa. Indirectly it also suggests that Vākpati fixed his capital at Dhārā. Here it is worth noting that of all these five rulers from Upēndrāraja to Vairisinha, the Nagpur prasasti gives only the last name, the Tilakamaṇāyari only that of Vairisinha, and the Navasāhasānika-charita which gives the name of Upēndrāraja, omits those of Vairisinha (I) and Siyaka (I). Thus the present inscription is the only record which gives a complete genealogy of the earlier Paramāra rulers of Mālwā, as already stated before.
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: The next three verses (13-15) speak of Siyaka's son Vākpatirāja, who is stated to have been well-versed in the Sāstras and a poet too. The N.S. Charita calls him Utpalarāja (XI, 92). In the Nagpur prasasti we have the name Muñja instead of Vākpati; and Hall recognises first the identity of the two names. The land-grants call him Vākpati and add that he was also known as Amōghavarsha and bore the titles of Prithvī-vallabha and Śrī-vallabha. The praise given by the present prasasti to Vākpati is not undeserved, as we know from the various quotations of his verses in anthologies, works on alaṅkāvas, the Prabandhacintāmaṇi and the Bhōjaprabandha, etc., though some of these may be of a doubtful nature.
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: In verse 8, which begins the genealogy, the inscription mentions the name Upēndrarāja, adding that he was born in the lineage of Paramāra and that “he acquired the high honour of kinghood by his prowess”. This indirectly goes to indicate that he was the first of the Paramāra kings of Mālwā. The land grants, on the other hand, mention the originator of the house to be Krishnarāja; and Dr. Hall and Cunningham have therefore taken both these names to be identical. Bühler also drew our attention to the fact that both these names are identical, and he further suggested that Upēndrarāja was probably the poetical form of the name and Krishnarāja was its Prakrit equivalent to be used in every day life.
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: Bhōjadēva, is eulogised in the prāśasti for his strength, charities, victories and temple-building activities, in vv. 16-20. The assertion of the prāśastikāra that Bhōja resembled Prithu' and ruled the earth from Kailāsa (in the north) to Malaya-gri (in the south), and from the mountain where the Sun rises to that where it sets (east and west respectively) is merely a poetic way of expression which is absolutely worthless for historical purposes. Verse 18 alludes to his knowledge and endows him with the title of kavurāja. The praise is not undeserved, since, as we know, a number of works were composed by Bhōja himself and his protégés. Verse 19 enumerates Bhōja's military exploits and victories won by him over the lord of Chēdis, Indraratha, Toggala(?) Bhūma, the king of the Gurjaras, the lord of Lāṭa, the Karnāṭas and the Turushkas.
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: Verse 20 of the prāsasti states that Bhōja ‘covered the world all around with temples dedicated to Kēdāra, Rāmēśvara, Sōmanātha, Sunḍīra (?), Kāla, Anala and Rudra.’ The first three of these names appear to be intended to refer, respectively, to the well-known Śiva temples in the north, south and west; and following the same, the fourth, which is a strange and so-far-unknown name, may possibly have been one in the east. Kāla, the fifth of the names enumerated here, may possibly be taken to be an abbreviated form of Mahākāla, at Ujjain; and the last two of the names, i.e., Anala and Rudra, which also are synonymous with Śiva are very common and cannot be specified. Commenting on this statement of the prāśasti, Bühler has rightly remarked that it cannot be corroborated, \( ^{5} \)  and agreeing with him, we are also inclined to hold that the choice of these names may have been made with a view to impress what the prāśasti has already stated in v.
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: The name of Jayasiniha is not known from any other inscription of the house—not even from the Udaipur and Nagpur prasats which give an almost complete list of kings ruling at Dhara up to the time when they were engraved. On the other hand, Bhojadêva is generally taken to have been succeeded by Udayadilva who is now definitely known to be his brother. But the present record, which mentions Jayasimha as the immediate successor of Bhojadêva and the evidence of which cannot be doubted for any reason, definitely shows that Jayasiniha must be placed between Bhojadêva and Udayadilva and thus between 1047 and 1080 A.C. which are respectively the latest and the earliest known years of these two rulers.
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: The inscription thus reveals for the first time a new historical fact, viz. that Lakshmadēva predeceased both Udayāditya and Naravarman, though the circumstances leading to his death, along with the approximate time when it took place, are not known. Here we have also to note that the Nagpur Museum stone inscription, which enumerates the names of all the rulers from Vairisinha to Lakshmadēva, while introducing each one of them, uses such a word as signifies 'a king', e.g., kshutipati, bhūpati or ūripa, but such a word is not used in it in the case of the last of them only, i.e. Lakshmadēva, though it states that he was devoted to govern the subjects. \( ^{4} \)  The omission of a word denoting a king only with the name of Lakshmadēva in the record is significant as it perhaps implies to show that he never ascended the throne of Dhāra. That he worked as governor in some of the eastern part of the Paramāra dominions under his father Udayāditya is also suggested by the donation made by him as recorded in the same inscription.
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: The inscription refers itself to Udayāditya who is endowed in it with the titles of Paramabhattāraka, Mahāvājādhiraja and Paramēśvara, and is stated to have then encamped at the village Dhavalī near Ujjain. \( ^{1} \)  The purpose of the inscription is to record the donation made by Naravarman, who was evidently his son, of 12 halas (?) of land in the village known as Rādhaghatikā, for perpetually burning a lamp (akshaya-dīpikā) in honour of Lakshmadēva who was another son of Udayāditya and thus a brother of Naravarman. The year, mentioned in numerical figures in the last line of the inscription, is 1140, without any further details. As the current Vikrama year, it corresponds to 1082 A.C. The name of the engraver is not recorded, nor is any epithet attached either to the name of Naravarman or to that of Lakshmadēva.

quote: The following verse (21) introduces Udayāditya, who is spoken of as 'another Sun dispelling the dense darkness in the form of his magnanimous foes with the rays issuing from his strong sword and thereby gladdening the hearts of his people by his splendour'. The enemies referred to here are not specified, but the description goes to indicate that they were very powerful and had deprived the Paramāras of their kingdom in the last days of Bhōja, or immediately after his death. From the Prabandhachintāmaṇi we learn that in the last days of Bhōjadēva the Kalachuri Karṇa and the Chaulukya Bhīma attacked Mālwā simultaneously and took possession of his kingdom. This statement is corroborated by epigraphical records of the Paramāras. The Nagpur prasasti, which is more explicit on the point, states that Udayāditya resembled the Great Boar in delivering the earth (i.e., the Paramāra kingdom) which had submerged in the mighty oceans in the form of the Karṇāta, Karṇa and others (prabhriti). This description agrees very closely with that of the Mándhātā grant of Jayasinīha II, though the enemy mentioned there was only the Gurjara king.

It has to be admitted here, however, that we have no evidence in support of this assertion, nor is it possible to fix the date of this clash. With reference to Vākpati’s victory over the Karnātaṣ (evidently the Chālukyas), we know that in his long struggle with his adversary Trailapa II, he had to lose his throne and life in the end; and the claim of the prasasti that Vākpati subdued the Karnāṭas is evidently inadmissible. It is however possible that he may have gained some success in one of his earlier expeditions against the region and that success may have been referred to here.

Bühler contends that the story of Bhōja's reverse narrated by the Prabandhachintāmaṇi and also by the epigraphical records of the house cannot be implicitly accepted because it does not find place in the inscriptions of the Kalachuris; nor does Hémachandra, who extols Bhima 'in the best possible light' and who wrote his Dvyāśraya-kāvya about 150 years before Mērutunga, say anything about it. But here we are to remember that it was a long-drawn war and the story does not end with the reverse sustained by Bhōja but with the 'total destruction (saṅhāra) of the Kalachuri king (Dāhal-ādhiśa) at the hands of Udayāditya,' as we know from 1.2 of the following inscription, which is in continuation of the inscription in hand and was discovered 37 years after Bühler worked out his article.
The next verse (22), which is the last complete verse of the prasasti, again glorifies Udayā-ditya, stating that 'for him who restored the earth (from the enemies) it was easy to restore the Premial Boar.' This statement appears to be a hint to the restoration of a Boar-temple by Udayāditya, as we shall see in the inscription that follows (Part B).

quote: But in these dark days there was one ray of light on the eastern horizon, which gradually expanded, and dispersed all the black clouds from the sky of Malwa. Udayāditya, a scion of a junior branch of the Paramāras, stood gallantly for the liberation of his ancestral dominion. In those perilous hours he appealed to the Câhamâna Durlabha III, the king of Sâkambhari, for assistance. book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
quote: When the Pratiharas' power weakened, three powers emerged. Among these, the Chedis of Kalachuri, the Chandelas of Jaijakabhukti, and the Paramaras of Malwa rise upon the horizon together. In their long span of five centuries, the ambitious Paramara kings extended their boundaries over a large territory. Their kingdom was spread — along with Malwa — up to Vidisha and Udaipur beyond Bhopal, and in the west up to areas like Hansol, Modhasa and Mahudi. In the south, the Paramaras were ruling over regions from the Narmada's coastal tracts, such as Hoshangabad, up to Kota in the north. Some branches of the Paramara dynasty of Malwa had succeeded in establishing their kingdoms in the Arbund Mandal — the Paramaras of Chandravati, and [those of] Bhinmal, Kiradu, Jalore and Bagar.

book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
quote: The period from the ninth to the fourteenth century, during which the Paramaras existed in this region, was itself such a time that the royal dynasties present all over India were carrying out the finest construction work in their kingdoms. From the Cholas far in the south to the Chandelas of Bundelkhand, from the Chauhans in Rajasthan to the Pala kings in Bengal-Bihar, the priceless heritage built by the contribution of generations was shining at its peak. Just as, in a match, runs are scored rapidly in the last over, so, on a war-footing, this construction work was done. After the eleventh century, this "over" was really about to end — as though destiny were constantly inspiring India's countless dynasties in every corner to gather all their energy and all the talent of their craftsmen, and to depart only after fashioning some unmatched specimens of craft for the coming generations. Wherever stone was available, no corner was left [untouched] for India's great creation.

उस दौर में राजपरिवार के अन्य महत्वपूर्ण सदस्यों को राजधानी से दूर के महत्वपूर्ण नगरों और सैन्य ठिकानों की कमान सौंपी जाती थी। एक तरह से राज्य शासन चलाने के पारिवारिक प्रशिक्षण का यह हिस्सा था और उत्तराधिकारियों को राज्यकार्य में दक्ष ऐसे ही बनाया जाता होगा। जैसे मध्य में सम्राट बनने के पहले अशोक के पिता बिंदुसार ने उन्हें अवंति का राज्यपाल बनाकर उज्जैन भेजा था।
*Gloss [my translation]:* In that period other important members of the royal family were entrusted with command of important towns and military bases far from the capital. In a way this was part of family training in running the state. Just as before becoming emperor Ashoka was sent to Ujjain by his father Bindusara as governor of Avanti.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
गुप्त काल में पहले इतिहासकारों का मानना था कि 'ततपादानुध्येत' शब्द सीधे उत्तराधिकारी की बात करता है। जैसे चंद्रगुप्त प्रथम, समुद्रगुप्त, चंद्रगुप्त द्वितीय विक्रमादित्य, कुमारगुप्त, स्कंदगुप्त और उसके आगे की वंश परंपरा में हर परवर्ती शासक स्वयं को अपने पूर्ववर्ती का तत पादानुध्येत कह कर संबोधित करता है।
परंतु काकनादबोट (साँची) और उदयगिरि के लेखों में क्रमशः आत्रकादवर्द और वीरसेन शाब को चंद्रगुप्त द्वितीय विक्रमादित्य का ततपादानुध्येत कहा गया जो सम्राट के विश्वस्त कमांडर थे। इससे यह माना गया कि इसका शब्दिक अर्थ "चरणों का ध्यान करता हुआ" अधिक उपयुक्त है। यह तारीफ का कसीदा है, जिसका उत्तराधिकार से कोई लेना-देना नहीं। इसलिए यहाँ शोरगढ़ अभिलेख से भोज से उदयादित्य को सीधे उत्तराधिकार मिलने का दावा कमजोर पड़ जाता है।
*Gloss [my translation]:* Earlier historians of the Gupta period believed that 'tatpadanudhyata' speaks directly of a successor. But in the Kakanadabota (Sanchi) and Udayagiri inscriptions, Atrakadavarda and Virasena Shaba are called tatpadanudhyata of Chandragupta II, who were trusted commanders. Hence the literal meaning 'meditating on the feet' was considered more apt; it is praise with no relation to succession. So the claim of direct succession from Bhoja to Udayaditya weakens here.
tier_note: T8 tradition / testimony: testimony and local tradition (Tiwari); memory, not the event

claim.value: padanudhyata = praise, not direct succession (as argued)

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
परमारों के राज में मंदिर सिर्फ पूजा-अनुष्ठान तक सीमित नहीं थे। वह स्थानीय स्तर पर एक नॉलेज सेंटर या पाठशालाओं के लिए भी उपयोग होते थे। बच्चों को वहीं अपने समय की समस्त विधाओं की शिक्षा दी जाती थी। धार, उज्जैन और मांडू के सरस्वती कंठाभरण इसके प्रमाण रहे हैं। चौक बाजार में पुराने भोपाल का ऐतिहासिक सभा मंडल भी, जो इसी उदयपुर के रचयिता और परमारों के राजवंश में राजा भोज के बाद हुए महाराज उदयादित्य ने ही बनवाया था।
*Gloss [my translation]:* Under Paramara rule temples were not limited to worship and rituals. At the local level they were also used as knowledge centres or schools. Children were taught there all the disciplines of their time. The Saraswati Kanthabharanas of Dhar, Ujjain and Mandu have been proof of this. The historic Sabha Mandal of old Bhopal in Chowk Bazaar was also built by Maharaja Udayaditya, the maker of this very Udaipur, who came after Raja Bhoj in the Paramara dynasty.
tier_note: T8 tradition / testimony: testimony and local tradition (Tiwari); memory, not the event

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
परमार जिस नौवीं से चौदहवीं सदी के दौरान इस इलाके में हुए, वह समय ही ऐसा था जब पूरे भारत में मौजूद राजवंश अपने राज्यों में बेहतरीन निर्माण कार्य कर रहे थे। दूर दक्षिण में चोलों से लेकर बुंदेलखंड के चंदेलों तक, राजस्थान में चौहानों से लेकर बंगाल-बिहार में पाल राजाओं तक पीढ़ियों के योगदान से निर्मित बेशाकीमती विरासत अपने चरम पर चमक रही थी।
*Gloss [my translation]:* The period from the ninth to the fourteenth century in which the Paramāras flourished in this region was a time when dynasties across India were doing excellent construction in their kingdoms. From the Cholas far in the south to the Chandellas of Bundelkhand, from the Chauhans in Rajasthan to the Pala kings in Bengal-Bihar, the precious heritage built by generations was shining at its peak.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
परमार वंश के सभी राजा कलाप्रिय थे। मंदिरों के निर्माण पूरे राज्य में चलते थे। भोजपुर की चट्टान से लेकर धारा नगरी, उज्जयनी, मंडपदुर्ग और ओंकारेश्वर तक कितने नाम गिनाएं। अगर परमारों के राज में कोई सबसे व्यस्त था तो वे आदर्शीय शिल्पकार थे। वे पत्थरों पर आश्चर्य उकेरते थे।
*Gloss [my translation]:* All kings of the Paramara dynasty were lovers of art. Temple construction went on across the kingdom: from the rock of Bhojpur to Dhara, Ujjayini, Mandapadurga and Omkareshwar. If anyone was busiest under Paramara rule it was the ideal craftsmen. They carved wonders in stone.
tier_note: T8 tradition / testimony: testimony and local tradition (Tiwari); memory, not the event

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
कलाप्रिय परमार राजाओं की प्रतिष्ठा का एक कारण यह भी था कि बड़े ही विद्या अनुरागी थे। भाषा, व्याकरण, कविता, नाटक, वास्तु, स्थापत्य, ज्योतिष, संगीत जैसी तमाम विधाओं के जानकार उनके आसपास हुआ करते थे। राजा भोज तो इन प्रतिभाशाली कला विशेषज्ञों के बीच स्वयं एक विद्वान की हैसियत रखते थे। ऐसे माहौल में जिन उदयदित्य की परवरिश हुई होगी, उनके आसपास भी बिल्कुल वैसा ही माहौल होना ही चाहिए था।
*Gloss [my translation]:* One reason for the repute of the art-loving Paramara kings was that they were great lovers of learning. Experts in language, grammar, poetry, drama, vastu, architecture, astrology and music were around them. Raja Bhoj himself was a scholar among these talents. The environment around Udayaditya, brought up in such an atmosphere, must have been the same.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
वैसे पहाड़ी ऊंचाइयों की बात करें तो ओंकारेश्वर और मंदाता में भी परमार राजाओं ने नर्मदा के तटों पर अपनी श्रद्धा शिल्प में प्रकट की थी। चंदेरी और ग्वालियर में भी पहाड़ों पर आस्था के स्मारक बनाए गए।
*Gloss [my translation]:* Speaking of hilltop heights, at Omkareshwar and Mandhata too the Paramara kings expressed their devotion in sculpture on the Narmada's banks. At Chanderi and Gwalior also monuments of faith were built on hills.
tier_note: T8 tradition / testimony: testimony and local tradition (Tiwari); memory, not the event
gloss: Speaking of hilltop heights, at Omkareshwar and Mandhata too the Paramara kings expressed their devotion in sculpture on the Narmada's banks. At Chanderi and Gwalior also monuments of faith were built on hills.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
वह एक चौकोर रचना में वास्तु के नियमों के तहत बसाया गया एक व्यवस्थित नगर था, जिसके बीचों-बीच आज का चौक बाजार रहा होगा। परमारों के समय यह सभामंडल था, नगर का महत्वपूर्ण ब्रह्मस्थान। यह एक विशाल मंदिर परिसर था, जो संस्कृत का विद्यालय भी था। बिल्कुल उज्जैन, धार और मांडू के महान् सरस्वती कंठाभरणों की तर्ज पर। लेकिन सभा मंडल का निर्माण भोज के बाद हुआ और उदयादित्य ने ही कराया।
*Gloss [my translation]:* It was an orderly city settled in a square design under the rules of vastu, with today's Chowk Bazaar probably at its centre. In Paramara times this was the Sabha Mandal, the city's important Brahmasthana. It was a vast temple complex that was also a Sanskrit school, on the lines of the great Sarasvati Kanthabharanas of Ujjain, Dhar and Mandu. But the Sabha Mandal was built after Bhoja and was made by Udayaditya himself.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
पत्थर की प्रचुर मात्रा में उपलब्धता ने परमार राजवंश को यह अवसर दिया कि वे स्थापत्य के शानदार नमूने खड़े करें। इस काम में परमार राजाओं ने जैसे तमिलनाडू के चोल राजाओं से मुकाबला किया है। अपने राज्य में हर कहीं बेमिसाल मंदिर, महल, तालाब, बावड़ियां, संस्कृत के शिक्षा केंद्र बनवाए।
*Gloss [my translation]:* The abundant availability of stone gave the Paramara dynasty the opportunity to raise splendid specimens of architecture. In this work the Paramara kings competed as it were with the Chola kings of Tamil Nadu. Everywhere in their kingdom they had matchless temples, palaces, tanks, stepwells and centres of Sanskrit learning built.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
आज के विदिशा की पुरानी बस्ती में सबसे खास तो वही विजय मंदिर है, जो परमार राजवंश के राजा नरवर्मन ने बनवाया था। परमारों की वंशावली में राजा नरवर्मन का क्रम राजा उद्यादित्य के बाद आता है। वे उनके उत्तराधिकारी थे। मुमकिन है कि उदयपुर के नीलकंठेश्वर महादेव के मंदिर निर्माण के समय युवा नरवर्मन उदयपुर में ही रहे हों और राजधानी धार में राजकाज संभालने के बाद उनका झुकाव इस क्षेत्र में बना रहा हो।
*Gloss [my translation]:* The most special thing in old Vidisha is the Vijay temple built by Paramara king Naravarman. In the Paramara genealogy Naravarman comes after Udayaditya; he was his successor. It is possible that young Naravarman lived in Udaipur at the time of building the Nilakantheshwar temple, and kept an inclination toward this region after ruling from Dhar.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
मगर परमारों के बारे में उसने हर जगह इज्जत से जिक्र किया। वह कहता है कि सेंट्रल इंडिया के इतिहास में पवार राजपूत अन्य राजवंशों से ज्यादा सम्माननीय माने जाते हैं। लेकिन उन्हें मुसलमानों ने हराया और बहुत समय पहले उनका राज्य खत्म हो गया। बाद में इस वंश का एक सरदार अपने पूर्वजों की राजधानी धार में स्थापित हो गया।
*Gloss [my translation]:* But about the Paramaras he mentioned them everywhere with respect. He says in Central India's history the Pawar Rajputs are considered more respectable than other dynasties. But they were defeated by Muslims and their kingdom ended long ago. Later a chief of this line settled in Dhar, their ancestors' capital.

quote: \( ^{1} \)  Verses 7-9 describe the scene of a battle which, from the description, appears to have been very fierce; and though the name of the Paramāra king who fought it is lost, he appears to have been no other than Siyaka II, from the fact that his son and successor Muñjadēva is described in the verses that immediately follow (10-12). Muñja is said to have been a valorous prince who defeated his enemies: these enemies are not mentioned by name, but they seem to have been the Chālukyas or the Chaulukyas with whom he is known to have waged wars. Verses 13-15 mention (Muñja's younger brother) Sindhurāja; and the next five verses (16-20) are devoted to the description of (his son) Bhōjadēva eulogising his learning and munificence in a conventional manner. After Bhōja is mentioned Jayasinha (lam-anu), who is stated to have been a great warrior vanquishing all his enemies; but the statement that he subjugated the earth bounded by the four oceans is again conventional and historically worthless.

quote:
The inscription refers itself to the reign of the illustrious Bhōjadēva who is called in it ‘the moon among the kings’ and who has been identified with the great literary person of that name and the king of Dhārā. The purpose of the inscription is to record the installation of the image of Vāgdevī, on the pedestal of which it is engraved. The year of the record, as mentioned in figures only and without any further details thereof, is 1091, which is equivalent to 1033-1034 A.C. The sculpture was engraved by Manathala, son of the mason Sahira, and the inscription was written by Sivadēva.
As we know from the Tilakamanjari, the palace of Bhōja or Bhōja-sālā as it is now popularly known, was then called Bhāratī-bhavana or Sarasvatīkaṇthābharaṇa, \( ^{3} \) and the image under reference may have been installed in it, in a prominent place, by Bhōja himself, who was a zealous devotee of the goddess Sarasvatī.

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote:
To review the contents of the record, the first of the two extant plates begins with the description of a king of the name of Bhōjadēva who slew numbers of the soldiers of his enemies by his valour and enjoyed a long reign. This statement is only in general terms and has no historical value. The name of the family of this ruler along with those of his predecessors appears to have been mentioned in the first plate which is lost; but it is not difficult to know that he was no other than the homonymous Paramāra king who issued the Mahauḍi and the other charters edited here and whose kingdom included in it the Sābarkāṃthā-Ahmedabad region, as we know from his grandfather Sīyaka's grants of the Harsōlā plates and from one of his feudatories at Mōḍāsā, which have been dealt with above.\( ^{2} \)
The inscription on then introduces the name of Bhōja's feudatory\( ^{3} \) Sūrāditya, who had migrated from Kānyakubja (Kanauj) and who had been born in the family of the Śravaṇabhadras. This hero is further stated to have killed his overlord's enemy warriors and thus rendered the sovereignty of the latter firm.

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: However, it may not be impossible that the word Sāhavāhana, which appears to be the same as Sātavāhana\(^{2}\) may have been used by the composer of the inscription in its general significance to denote the southerners; and this at once brings to our mind the Western Chālukyas who were then ruling over the Deccan as successors of the Sātavāhanas and who are known to have been the hereditary enemies of the Paramāras. Following this line of thought it is not impossible to hold that this allusion may have a reference to Bhōja's war with the Chālukya Jayasimha, who is represented in one of his inscriptions as "the moon of the lotus which was king Bhōja"\(^{3}\), or it may refer to Bhōja's conquest of Kōnkaṇa as referred to in his Beṭmā and Bānswādā grants, as seen above. But owing to the absence of any reliable source of information, the precise significance of the term Sāhavāhana cannot be definitely known. It is, however, certain that Bhōja succeeded in extending the southern boundaries of his kingdom.

Bhōja's success over the Karmṇātakas obviously refers to the long-drawn war which began from the time of Vākpati-Muñja and Tailapa.

It would thus appear that Bhōja's struggle with all his enemies mentioned in the present record has reference to his warfare effected during the time between the Bētmā and Bānswādā grants and that of Jayasimha at whose hands he had to suffer a reverse. At any rate, it may be taken to have been much before Bhōja's last days when he had to suffer a reverse at the hands of most of his enemies.

The object of it is to record the grant, by Jayasimhadēva, of the village Bhima, situated in the territorial division of Maktulā-forty-two in the Pūrnapathaka-mangala, for the maintenance of the Brāhmaṇas residing in the patta-sālā (tent-house) at the holy Amarēśvara, for the religious merit of his parents and himself. quote: The Prabandhachintāmaṇi tells us that in the last days of Bhōja the Kalachuri Karṇa and the Chaulukya Bhāma made an alliance against him and invaded Mālwā, respectively from the east and the west and took possession of his kingdom. \( ^{1} \)  As we have seen above, Bhōja's unfortunate end is also hinted at in the Udaipur prasasti; and we know that in that predicament his successor Jayasinha regained his hereditary kingdom through the help of the Chālukya king Sōmeśvara-Ahavamalla, who sent his son Vikramāditya VI to help him against the enemies. \( ^{2} \)  The expression nājye cha kuly-ākule in the verse under reference may also hint at some internal disturbance in the Paramāra kingdom after Bhōja had deceased, and Kielhorn's suggestion that it was 'possibly crowded with nobles' appears to be correct in view of the use of the particle cha in the first foot of the verse.

quote: Considering this, I am inclined to hold that the Karṇāta king mentioned in the present inscription appears to be Ereyānga and Karṇa was no other than the Kalachuri king who had once before invaded Mālwā but was repulsed by the Chālukya Vikramāditya coming for Jayasiniha's help, as just seen. The word pūbhijti of the verse under reference thus appears to denote the other king to be the Gaṅga Udayāditya. Both these inscriptions too do not contain a word about the imperial king. On the other hand, if Bhōja's conquest of Kōknāṇa is to be placed some time between 1018 and 1020 A.C., the former being the year of his Mahaudī grant which does not mention this achievement and the latter of those found at Bētmā and Bānswādā which are explicit on the point, it is obvious that his power was then rather increasing; and knowing from history that he had to suffer only towards the end of his rule in the combined attack on his kingdom by the Chaulukyas and the Kalachuris and some time before, at the hands of the Chālukyas, it is difficult to agree with Banerji in his conclusion. quote: Moreover, the statement of the Bhopāl grant of Udayavarman to the effect that Lakshmīvarman succeeded in occupying the territory not from Jayavarman, who, as we have seen in the preceding grant, had himself fled to the Bhopāl region and may have then been accompanied by Lakshmīvarman, but from his enemies who were the Chandēlas who had by that time usurped a portion of the region around Bhilsā, as we know from the Augasī grant of Madanavarman,\(^{3}\) which was issued from his residence near Bhillasānipura: and our observation gets further support from the fact that Lakshmīvarman confirmed the grant made by his father in the same region around Bhilsā which is herein called the Mahādvādaśaka-mandala: and it may fairly be imagined that Lakshmīvarman's reconquest of the region may probably have necessitated the re-issuing of the grant.

quote: and resumed the government, proclaiming himself as a sovereign lord: and the younger brother Lakshmīvarman continued to remain in the Bhopāl region as a subordinate ruler, where he and his descendants governed the territory and were satisfied with the lower title of Mahā-kumāru. Professor Hall's theory that Lakshmīvarman was the elder of the two,\(^{1}\) cannot be accepted as it is not based on any substantial evidence: and the very fact that Jayavarman is called a Mahārajādhiñāja not only in his but also in the grants issued by the Mahākumāras who were the descendants of Lakshmīvarman, goes against Hall's observations.

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: Hariśchandra, the son of Lakshmīvarman, is known to have issued a grant from the same place vidishā, only a couple of years earlier in the (Vikrama) year 1214: and in view of all these findings the only conclusion that can be drawn is that Trailōkyavarman of the present inscription undoubtedly belonged to that branch of the Paramāras who called themselves Mahā-kumāras in their inscriptions and the earliest of whom is known to be Lakshmīvarman. \( ^{2} \)  This again goes to support the view that Trailōkyavarman appears to have acted as a regent during the minority of his nephew Harischandra, and as such, he also enjoyed the titles connected with the princes of the Mahākumāra line and had full powers of a chief. \( ^{3} \)  This finds strange corroboration in the fact that in his Bhopāl grant Harischandra states that he obtained his rulership through the favour of the Mahākumāra Trailōkyavarman.

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: The grant was made, as seen above, on the ninth day of a month, the name of which is lost along with the figures showing the year, at the end of 1.2, by the Mahākumāra Trailōkyavarma-dēva, who is mentioned as samasta-prakriyā-virājamāna and also bearing all the royal titles. The pedigree of this prince and the name of the house to which he belonged are not specified in the record; but from the title of Mahākumāra attached to his name in it, he is evidently to be considered a member of the subordinate branch of the Paramāra house ruling over the region around Bhopāl and may be identified with the homonymous prince mentioned in the Bhopāl charter of the Paramāra Mahākumāra Harischandradeva, who is stated to have achieved his victory and kingship through this prince (-prasād-āvāpta-vujay-ādhupatyah).

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: In view of this consideration, it does not appear to be impossible that Harischandra was very young when he succeeded his father Lakshmivarman, as also pointed out by Chakravarti. Moreover, we may also hold with the same scholar that during Harischandra’s minority, his uncle, Trailōkyavarman, acted as a regent, and as such, he also enjoyed the titles connected with the princes of this line and wielded the full power of a chief who could also issue a grant.

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: The charter then refers to the predecessors of the donor, giving the names of the Paramabhattāraka, Mahārājādhirāja and Paramēśvara, the glorious Naravarmadēva and his successor the P.M.P. the illustrious Yasōvarmadēva (ll. 3-4). After Yasōvarmadēva we have the names of Trailōkyavarmadēva and then of the doner Haríschandradēva, each of whom is mentioned as endowed with all praise and enjoying the right to the five great musical sounds. The record also supplies the additional information that the later of these two rulers obtained his principality through the favour of the former (-pāda-prasād-avāpla-vijay-adhapatyah).

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: Comparing the evidence supplied by the present and the following grants of Harischandra, we notice another inconsistency, viz., that whereas the former of these charters states that Harischandra obtained his territory through the favour of the Mahākumāra Trailōkyavarman, the latter gives this credit not to Trailōkyavarman but to the P.M.P. Jayavarman. But here we have to note the actual wordings of the two grants; for whereas the former uses the expression vujay-ādhuṣatya, meaning that Harischandra obtained some victory (over an enemy), the latter has the expression nij-ādhuṣatya, indicating that he received the principality from (through the sanction of) Jayavarman who was then the Imperial sovereign. To obtain sanction of the Imperial house, which was ruling at Dhārā, by the subordinate ruler in the Bhopāl region may have been a matter of necessity; and the Pipliānagar grant points to the same. The victory referred to in the present charter may possibly allude to one against the Chandēlas who were their northern neighbours.

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: Like many other Paramāra grants, the present record opens with two verses in honour of the god Śiva, and they are followed by prose passages containing the genealogy of the donor, mentioning the names of the Paramabhattāraka, Mahārājādhirāja and Paramēśvara Udayāditya, his successor the P.M.P. Naravarman, his successor the P.M.P. Yaśōvarman, and the latter's successor Jayavarman. This genealogy is the same as known from the other records of the house. But the information that follows is new; it states that Hariśchandra, who enjoyed the five great sounds and was a Mahākumāra, obtained his principality through the last-mentioned ruler, i.e., Jayavarman (ētasmāt-prishtatama-prabhōh prasād-āvāpta-nijādhipathy).

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: The importance of the present record, however, lies in the fact that it tells us that Hariśchandra was the son of Lakshmīvarman, as mentioned in the sign-manual of the king in the end. In fact this is the only record to mention this relationship. Another importance of the present inscription lies in the fact that Hariśchandra succeeded in extending the boundaries of his kingdom to the south of the Narmadā, as we shall see below while identifying the localities mentioned therein. For whereas all the other grants made by the rulers of the Mahākumāra branch of the Paramāra house refer to the region lying to the north of the river, the present one is the only grant made by a prince belonging to that house in the Hoshangābād District, which extends to the south of the Narmadā.

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: The genealogical portion (ll. 3 ff.) mentions the names of Yasōvarman and his successor Jayavarman, both as sovereign lords: and thereafter figures the name of Lakshmivarman, who is stated to have the privilege of using the five great sounds and was a Mahākumāra. He was succeeded by Harischandra, and Harischandra by his son Udayavarman,\(^{2}\) who issued the present grant. Both these rulers are mentioned as Mahākumāras, entitled to the use of the five great sounds, as Lakshmīvarman. Of the names figuring in the genealogy, those of Yasōvarman and his son Jayavarman, who were sovereign lords at Dhārā, are well known, and we also know that Lakshmīvarman was the latter's brother and had established himself in the Bhopāl

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: Referring to that history, we know that Jayavarman's son Vindhyavarman succeeded in recovering his ancestral dominions from the Chaulukya Mūlarāja II, but he could not do so before the present grant was issued; for had he succeeded finally establishing himself in Mālvā, we would have, as rightly suggested by Dr. N. P. Chakravarti, found his name mentioned in the present grant. \( ^{1} \)  He had also to fight hard against his southern neighbours who were at that time rising, viz., Bhillama V of the Yādava house of Dēvagiri and Ballāla II Dōrāsamudra, \( ^{5} \)  before he could completely assert his authority over Mālvā.

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: Verse 11 of the present record tells us that Yaśōvarman had a son named Ajayavarman (tasnād = Ajayaavarm = ābhāt); this expression is reproduced in the following two inscriptions of the king and in the Māndhāta grant of Devapāla and Jayavarman \( ^{2} \) ; whereas in the other set of records which are all in prose, \( ^{3} \)  the name of Yaśōvarman's son appears as Jayavarman; and this led Kielhorn to hold that Yaśōvarman had two sons with the names of Jayavarman and Ajayavarman who were two different persons. \( ^{4} \)  But when we consider that there is not even a single inscription which mentions both these names and also that there are two different sets of records—all those which are in prose invariably give the name to be Jayavarman and all those which are in poetry give it as Ajayavarman, the identity of both these persons is established beyond doubt, and it also follows that in the latter of these sets the name Jayavarman is changed to Ajayavarman only to suit the metre.
